text:
In one of the scenes in Nitesh Tiwari’s Ramayana: Part 1, Ram (Ranbir Kapoor) asks what the purpose of his birth is. He is vulnerable, confused, and deeply shaken by the odds that have consecutively been stacked against him. It is only in those fleeting moments, towards the end of the film, that we get some insight into the protagonist’s conflict in an adaptation that is otherwise deliberately held back. And this denial of interiority is neither without purpose nor limited to Ram.

Nitesh’s cinematic iteration of Valmiki’s epic anchors itself on caution. Everything is calculated, tepid even, in what seems like an attempt to prevent the story from making any detour that may offend bhakts or stir up controversy. But in its anxiety to avoid transgression, the film also relinquishes the artistic freedom to complicate inherited truths. By doing so, it reveals itself as a propaganda machine which flattens the interpretative potential of art and instead makes it a vehicle for cultural consolidation.

The irony, then, is hard to miss. In trying meticulously to offend no one, Nitesh Tiwari’s Ramayana: Part 1 appears to have not pleased people either. 

For viewers who lean towards a more liberal political spectrum, the lack of explicit right-wing messaging seems to be disarming. The lack of deliberation in pushing Hindutva on a scale that was anticipated appears to have somehow become the merit of the film for them. Their criticism is more about other aspects like acting, visual language, effects and so on.

The harsher criticism of the film, however, has been from the right-wing political ecosystem, which has forever championed the epic as India’s moral “truth” and Ram as the keeper of that conscience. This politicisation of the myth has found legitimacy through the 2019 Ram Janmabhoomi–Babri Masjid land dispute verdict of the Supreme Court and the subsequent installation of the Ram Mandir in Ayodhya. Therefore, any adaptation of the epic on screen must live up to the exactions of this ecosystem if it wishes to survive. 

Nitesh Tiwari does pander to that overarching context by giving us a detached, expressionless, ever-righteous Ram who embodies godliness from childhood. However, that does not seem to be enough.

If we dig deeper into the layers of the right-wing critique of the film, it becomes evident how peculiar the trap of propaganda is. For an industry that spared no opportunity to reproduce divisive political narratives under the garb of patriotism, censored films that questioned majoritarian state excess, and isolated filmmakers who tried to dissent, this is an entrapment of its own making.

When filmmakers help turn cinema into an instrument of ideological conformity, they eventually find themselves unable to satisfy even those they set out to appease. 

Nitesh and team have no wiggle room, despite not even attempting to make any. The end result is an understated film adaptation of an epic, which has neither been able to take imaginative liberties nor reap the fruits of its calculated restraint.

‘This is Ravanayana’

Ramayana: Part 1 begins with the war between the devtas and the asuras. Relegated to the underground by Indra, the asuras suffer for centuries before Ravana (Yash) reinstates their dignity. The film spends considerable screen time on this origin story, following Ravana through his boyhood to adulthood, when he finally becomes the lord of all three worlds. 

Nitesh attempts to delve slightly deeper into the making of this villain, whose masculine excess and thirst for power eventually trigger the main events of the Ram-Ravana clash. However, what would otherwise come across as character establishment has now become a point of contention for many viewers. The reason being that Ravana stands out in contrast to his carefully sanitised, prim and proper opponent, Ram of Ayodhya.

“Watched Namit Malhotra’s Ramayana. A flop of a film being discussed only because it bears a superficial resemblance to the Ramayana! What is promoted is essentially a Dravidianist, feminist and socialist interpretation of a Ravanayanam. Rama is reduced to a sorry figure, with a hunchback and an expressionless, stone-like face,” wrote a viewer on social media platform X.

“This is less Ramayana and more Ravanyana. Ravana has undeniably been glorified. One need only look at the number of children who, after watching the film, have begun praising Ravana to understand the impression it leaves,” wrote another viewer on X.

The criticism is primarily rooted in the presentation of Ravana as “liberal”. Though the film’s casteist visual language ensures that the asuras are made to look less milk-skinned and their women less clothed than the people of Ayodhya, the criticism is that Ravana is not cruel enough. 

Actor Nitish Bharadwaj, former BJP MP who played Lord Krishna in BR Chopra’s television adaptation of the Mahabharat, wrote, “...By depicting a very liberal, socially just & fair Ravan, the film has nullified the basic purpose of Mahavishnu taking the Ram avatar to establish maryada!... This film cannot be an international representative of Indian cinema because it propagates a wrong narrative about Bharat’s history, heritage & core spiritual values.”

Essentially, what Nitish and several others from the right-wing ecosystem say is that by showcasing the vulnerabilities of Ravana, the film has humanised him instead of emphasising how barbaric he and his clan of asuras were.

“This is the purpose of this movie, is & they have achieved it: Making "Ravan" the Hero. The makers of "Ramayana" are too happy with this review. They will spend even 12000 crore rupees to brainwash the Hindu next generation. Shame on those Hindus who went to watch this movie,” wrote another viewer on X.

It is anyone’s guess where this critique comes from. Brahmanical patriarchy leaves no room to humanise the marginalised, even if the purported upper caste saviour hero has been deified in all possible ways.

The lack of a certain machismo in Ram on screen, it appears, was meant to reinforce spiritual detachment and godly foresight. A choice Nitesh and his team may have made to not malign this ideal hero whose purported existence has now transcended the realm of mythology into reality. But that choice, though meant to elevate Ram as an undisputed icon of Hindutva, and by extension, India, seems to have sorely backfired.

Not only did the restraint irk those who were perhaps waiting to see a Dhurandhar-esque Ram, seething with pride and revenge, but it also disappointed fans of Ranbir Kapoor, who say the actor was given nothing to perform. 

The criticism, though, is not limited to how the men were portrayed. There is another section it takes on, and rather mercilessly: the women in the film.

‘Sita addresses Ram by his name?’

Ramayana: Part 1 is perhaps the first cinematic version of the epic in which we see a sword-wielding Sita (Sai Pallavi). The character is introduced as a knowledgeable woman who is also trained in combat. In the Aaranyakandh, where Ram, Lakshman, and Sita wade their way through a bewilderingly plastic VFX forest, she is seen to defend herself when needed. Though Ram swoops in to save her, Sita, in several scenes, is presented as having a mind and personality of her own.

This has, however, become another point of contention for several far-right groups who think that Nitesh Tiwari has made Sita “feminist” – a word that is a synonym for all things reprehensible in their glossary. 

“Can’t believe some educated hindus are supporting a #Ramayana where Sita ji is scolding lakshman for cutting off innocent surpankha’s nose, Laxman is apologizing and Ram ji accepts surpanakha is the victim,” wrote a viewer on social media platform X.

To contextualise this, Ramayana: Part 1 depicts Ravana’s sister Surpanakha as a woman in a troubled marriage. It is after the murder of her husband Vidyuth that she spots Ram in the forest and becomes besotted by him. As she tries to woo him, disguised as Sita, Lakshman chops her nose off. Sita immediately reprimands him, pointing out how disproportionate his reaction was, and why disfiguring a woman is not befitting of a man with integrity.

If you look at this scene, it essentially adds to the moral compass Sita upholds. The same stance, if taken by a man, would earn him brownie points. But here, many right-wingers have taken offence, interpreting this as the filmmaker’s attempt to justify Ravana and infantilise Ram.

Many of them have also been extremely uncomfortable with Sita addressing Ram by his name and not adjectives like Aaryaputhr or Swami, as we have seen in earlier adaptations.

Similarly, the physical abduction of Sita has been omitted in the film. We see Ravana in disguise, manipulating Sita to step out of the Lakshmanrekha, and then, we see her in his pushpak vimaan. There is no visualisation of how Ravana actually put her in his vehicle. This is probably a choice Nitesh made to either not show graphic violence against a woman on screen, or to not malign Sita, who has attained godliness akin to Ram’s in people’s minds.

This too, however, has stirred fury.

“Some clown YouTubers are claiming that they couldn’t show Sita Haran the way it is described in Valmiki Ramayana because people would get offended by how brutal it is. But why would people be offended by Ravana being portrayed as an evil, ruthless demon? People have already watched Ramanand Sagar’s Ramayan, where Ravana literally abducts Mata Sita by force. Go and see for yourself how that scene was portrayed! The truth is, they wanted to give Ravana a softer portrayal, and that’s exactly why they butchered one of the most important scenes,” noted a film and pop culture page on X. 

“Feminist Sai pallavi couldn't cry for help when abducted, was even wondering why Jatayu died. Next is she asking Raavan to cook his food himself for gender equality and she will drive pushpak,” noted another viewer on X.

Actor Sai Pallavi too has been subjected to cyberattacks for not “looking beautiful enough”. Several online pages have made numerous posts on how Kajal Agarwal, who plays Ravana’s wife Mandodari, should have played Sita, because “she looks better than Sai Pallavi”.

In effect, if one were to tie together all the arguments against Ramayana: Part 1 from the right-wing, it shows that even a relatively cautious adaptation that takes pains to preserve Ram's divinity can still be accused of ideological betrayal.

A demon of their own making

The Ramayana is an epic that has formed the basis of storytelling for decades owing to its narrative richness. And the history of Ramayana adaptations is also a history of departures. 

For example, Mani Ratnam’s Raavanan (2010) anchored itself on police excess and marital discord, while G Aravindan’s Kanchana Sita (1977) emphasised a feminist lens on the epic. Even Karan Johar’s Bollywood blockbuster Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham (2001) is read to have taken its core conflict from the epic.

Though these versions of Ramayana would invariably invite offence from religious puritans, they are insulated by the fact that they are adaptations, set in entirely different contexts. Ramayana: Part 1 does not get that leeway because now, what is on screen is not just storytelling, but a sort of deity worship.

It is important to reflect on where cinema as an artistic medium stands in the middle of this. If every deviation is an affront, what remains of storytelling?

Even while promoting the film, Nitesh and his team made sure that there was a certain piety in their clothing and their conversations. Back in 2023, when Adipurush, another film version of the Ramayana, was released, the filmmakers urged everyone to leave a seat vacant in theatres for Hanuman, who is believed to have no death. There has also been considerable noise about which woman actor must play Sita on screen, because whoever takes that up must be “morally fit” to play a deity’s wife.

Therefore, there is a peculiar irony when an industry that has helped turn myth into political property now discovers that it can no longer exercise artistic ownership over it. 

The right-wing prescription and backlash over Ramayana: Part 1 is, of course, unfair. But it is hard to place its makers and actors as victims because this is a demon of a complacent industry’s own making. It remains to be seen how they would take the franchise forward from here– by passing the ideological litmus test or discovering that there are only newer ways to fail. ",

New Delhi: The epic tale of Ram and Sita is back in the spotlight in India’s most expensive film to date.

BBC delves into the enduring hold of the Ramayana as Namit Malhotra and Nitesh Tiwari bring it back to the big screen.. 

The film may have received mixed reviews, but has turned heads within India and outside nonetheless.

Meanwhile, China’s Global Times comments on the growing debate over Beijing’s export controls on tunnel boring machines, and the India link.



In a report for the BBC, Zoya Mateen looks at the release of Part 1 of Ramayana: Rise of a Legend, and the expectations surrounding its attempt to take one of Hinduism’s foundational epics to a global audience. Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, the film has critics divided over whether its VFX-laden visual spectacle does justice to the story.

But the film’s significance goes beyond its critical reception. In India, the film—starring Ranbir Kapoor, Sai Pallavi and Yash—has invited comparisons with earlier adaptations, especially Ramanand Sagar’s Ramayan, which “captivated the country nearly four decades ago with simple sets and special effects that now seem quaint”.

When the television series first aired in 1987, it became a national phenomenon. “Streets emptied, shops lowered their shutters and neighbours crowded around TV sets. Some viewers bathed, lit incense and garlanded their screens before the broadcast, preparing for the show much as they might for worship,” Mateen writes.

Arvind Rajagopal, a media scholar at New York University, told the BBC in 2019 that “trains and buses would stop and passengers disembark to watch the show on roadside TVs”.

The report also recalls the 1992 Indian-Japanese animated film Ramayana: The Legend of Prince Rama, which brought the epic to life through richly detailed, hand-drawn animation. The film was an Indian-Japanese collaboration, combining an Indian epic with Japanese animation techniques and storytelling traditions.

“Tiwari’s Ramayana arrives with technological resources its predecessors could barely have imagined—but also with the expectations of generations who have grown up with the story and its characters,” Mateen adds.

The expectations are not just cultural, but also political. “It also comes at a politically charged moment in India, where Ram has become a powerful symbol of Hindu identity—over the past decade and a half, even popular analyses or retellings of the epic have landed in controversy.” The 2023 film Adipurush—another big-budget retelling of the Ramayana, starring Prabhas, Kriti Sanon and Saif Ali Khan—had sparked backlash over its portrayal of religious figures, dialogue and visual effects.

Meanwhile, writing in The Guardian, Peter Bradshaw calls the newly released Ramayana a “thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama”. He found echoes of Shakespeare in the royal intrigue that sends Ram into exile, and of Homer in his quest to rescue Sita, Mateen notes.

But Siddhant Adlakha of IGN was not so impressed. He scored the film four out of 10. For him, the action sequences were “clunky” and the computer-generated imagery (CGI) an “eye-sore”.

The use of AI to adjust lip movements of actors for the English version has also been criticised. For Tiwari, the idea was to make the film more accessible to international viewers, BBC report adds, but Adlakha describes it as “exaggerated mouth movements superimposed on still images for comedy sketches”.

The report also captures the weight of the roles for the actors. Ranbir Kapoor, who plays Ram, told the BBC that he was “filled with fear”, playing Lord Ram on the big screen.

How the film is received will become clearer as audiences head to cinemas. “But whatever the verdict, it marks a major cultural moment for India, bringing a story loved for generations to the big screen on an unprecedented scale,” Mateen writes.



In an editorial titled ‘A single TBM should not become a source of friction between China and India’, the Global Times responds to the debate over China’s export controls on tunnel boring machines, arguing that the issue should not become another source of tension between New Delhi and Beijing.

India’s Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal recently said that if China did not supply TBMs, India would develop them domestically, insisting that “India is not one to bow down”. The remarks received coverage in Indian and Western media, with several portraying the issue as “India refusing to yield to China’s ‘chokehold’”.

China announced the export controls on 19 October, with measures due to take effect on 18 November.

The editorial clarifies that the announcement “does not name any country”, and that the controls “are not directed at any specific party”. It stresses that “the measures centre on licensing rather than an outright export ban”. Applications for compliant exports to legitimate civilian projects, it says, will be approved provided the end users and end uses are clearly identified and meet the relevant requirements.

Global Times acknowledges, “India may have some misunderstandings or even complaints about these measures, and that is understandable”. It points out that “the country is in the midst of an intensive infrastructure-building drive”, and that, whether for metro networks, high-speed rail projects, highways or water conservancy tunnels, “India has considerable demand for large-scale excavation equipment such as TBMs”.

However, it argues that “there is little need to politicise a routine export-control matter”, let alone turn it into a question of whether India will “never bow down”, or defend its “national dignity”. Dismissing speculation that China is deliberately seeking to “restrict India’s use of TBMs in border areas”, the editorial says such claims “say more about the insecurity of those making them than about China’s intentions”.

It warns that “a confrontational mindset will only narrow the space for pragmatic consultations, ultimately jeopardising India’s own infrastructure projects and development progress”.

At the same time, it says India’s pursuit of “self-reliance” and efforts to build domestic TBM manufacturing capabilities are legitimate aspirations, while China has “an equally legitimate right to safeguard its national security and fulfill its international obligations”. Global Times adds: “China has never viewed India’s development as a threat to itself.” It also insists that “China is not that ‘petty’”.

Taking aim at Western coverage, the Global Times says certain US media outlets have shown particular “enthusiasm” for the issue. It mentions Bloomberg‘s description of the export controls as “a trade war risk to India”, while accusing The New York Times of portraying China’s industrial strengths as a “source of economic leverage” and claiming that “Beijing was building up its arsenal of economic weapons”.

The editorial further argues that such coverage seeks to “drive a wedge between China and India”, urging the two countries to address the issue through technical channels, rather than allow it to undermine broader bilateral relations.

The internet had already made up its mind about Ramayana long before November 5. The VFX looked artificial, the reported Rs 4,000 crore budget invited ridicule, Ranbir Kapoor was supposedly the wrong choice for Rama, and Sai Pallavi had to endure scrutiny over her suitability to play Sita. Even the music, composed by AR Rahman and Hans Zimmer, was being dissected before audiences could experience it in context. To put it simply, a film that began as perhaps the most anticipated Indian cinematic spectacle, touted as India's answer to Hollywood, had become one of the most trolled and written-off films even before its release.

For a film carrying the weight of one of India's most revered epics, the expectations were enormous. Every promotional frame was scrutinised, and every creative decision became an invitation for another online argument.

But the theatrical release has forced a rethink. Those who saw merit in the film beyond the targeted noise now have reason to feel vindicated. The conversation around Ramayana has changed considerably, with several aspects receiving appreciation that seemed almost impossible a day before its release. This does not mean the film is without flaws or that every criticism was misplaced. However, there are things the internet got spectacularly wrong, perhaps almost as badly as Kaikeyi misunderstood Rama.
1. From AI jokes to jaw-dropping visuals

If there was one criticism that dominated the promotional campaign, it was the visual effects. Social media users questioned how a film reportedly mounted on a Rs 4,000 crore budget could have forests, creatures and backgrounds that looked artificial. Some even compared the footage to AI-generated imagery. The criticism was not entirely misplaced. Certain promotional shots looked unfinished, and the makers gave audiences enough reason to question the final output.

But watching the finished film is a different experience. DNEG, the eight-time Academy Award-winning visual effects company, has played a significant role in creating the film's visual world. And the difference is evident in some of its most ambitious sequences. The Jatayu-Ravana encounter, in particular, is a breathtaking piece of filmmaking. The scale, creature animation, movement and emotional stakes come together to create a sequence that can comfortably stand alongside international fantasy spectacles.

Many other action set pieces, including the Tadaka action set pieces and other forest confrontations are equally impressive. The film's attempt to create a mythological world with formidable creatures, elaborate environments and large-scale battles largely pays off.

Of course, not everything works. Certain Asuras still look artificial, and some CGI-heavy environments appear excessively polished. But reducing the entire film to cheap AI imagery is a criticism that the theatrical version has convincingly challenged. The promotional footage was not the finished product, and perhaps the internet should have waited before handing out its VFX report card.
2. Beneath the spectacle lies a heart

There was another concern surrounding Ramayana: would it be all spectacle and no soul? For an epic that has survived generations through its emotional relationships, the fear was understandable. The Ramayana is not merely about divine weapons, extraordinary creatures and spectacular battles. It is equally about duty, sacrifice, family and the difficult choices that define its characters.

The film does find that emotional foundation, even if it does not consistently explore it. Some of its strongest moments are surprisingly intimate. The confrontation surrounding Rama's exile and his relationship with Kaikeyi are among them. Lara Dutta's Kaikeyi is not reduced to a convenient antagonist, while Ranbir's Rama responds with an affection that makes their relationship more complicated than a simple victim-and-villain equation.

There is also a beautiful father and son moment between Dasharatha and Rama. As the king holds his son and seeks forgiveness, Rama gently holds his father's hand. It is a small gesture, but it communicates more than an elaborate monologue could. Rama telling Kaikeyi that she should feed him when he returns from exile is another understated detail that gives their relationship warmth.

The forest conversations between Rama and Lakshmana also offer welcome breathing space. These moments remind audiences that the characters are brothers before they become participants in an epic conflict.

Emotional writing is not equally effective everywhere, and certain relationships could have received greater depth. But the argument that the film is merely a VFX demonstration does not hold up when its quietest scenes are among its most affecting.
3. Sai Pallavi silences the casting doubts

Sai Pallavi's casting attracted considerable discussion even before the film's release. As often happens when actors take on characters embedded in India's cultural memory, the conversation moved beyond performance and into questions of appearance, styling and suitability.

The theatrical release gives a more convincing answer. Sai Pallavi brings grace and conviction to Sita without reducing her to an ornamental presence in Rama's journey. She is compassionate, but not passive; devoted, but not without agency. The forest sequences give her opportunities to demonstrate courage, while her interactions with Rama establish a relationship built on affection and mutual respect.

What works particularly well is her restraint. She does not turn Sita into an excessively theatrical character, nor does she rely on exaggerated expressions to communicate her strength.

There is always a danger of judging actors playing mythological characters against the performances that audiences grew up watching. Sai Pallavi largely avoids that trap by offering her own interpretation. She may not silence every debate about the character's portrayal, but she makes a strong case for the casting.
4. Beyond the big three, an ensemble shines

The pre-release conversation was understandably dominated by Ranbir Kapoor, Sai Pallavi and Yash. But an epic cannot function like a three-character drama. Its world depends on the people surrounding its central figures, and the film's extended cast deserves considerably more attention.

Arun Govil as Dasharatha is an interesting casting choice. The actor who became synonymous with Rama through Ramanand Sagar's 1987 television adaptation now plays his father. More importantly, he brings emotional weight to the king's helplessness and his separation from his son. Lara Dutta's Kaikeyi and Sheeba Chaddha's Manthara help establish the circumstances that lead to the exile. Ravie Dubey is another pleasant surprise as Lakshmana. He captures the character's loyalty, protectiveness and occasional impulsiveness, particularly in his interactions with Rama.

Rakul Preet Singh's Surpanakha brings intensity to an important character, while Kajal Aggarwal's Mandodari, Shobana's Kaikasi, Vivek Oberoi's Vidyutjihva and the actors playing Kumbhakarna and Vibhishana contribute to the larger world of Lanka.

Yash, however, deserves a separate mention. His Ravana is arguably the film's biggest crowd-puller. His screen presence, intensity and theatricality have become major talking points. There is an interesting contrast here: Ranbir's Rama is being judged against the expectations attached to a revered figure, while Yash's Ravana has more room for a dramatic interpretation. That does not automatically make one performance better than the other, but it explains why Ravana is dominating so much of the online conversation.
5. Ranbir Kapoor finds his Ram

Of all the casting decisions, Ranbir Kapoor's remains the most closely scrutinised. His off-screen image, previous roles and the expectations attached to playing Rama made him an easy target for pre-release criticism. There were doubts about whether he could shed his familiar screen persona and embody a character associated with restraint, dignity and righteousness.

Ranbir's answer is to play Rama differently rather than imitate earlier portrayals. His performance is built around stillness, with controlled expressions, measured movements and composed body language. What makes it work is that he never appears to be struggling to fit into an established image of Rama. Instead, he seems to have found his own interpretation of the character and simply inhabits it. He does not constantly try to communicate divinity. Rather, he portrays a prince who understands his responsibilities and accepts difficult choices without unnecessary theatrics. His interactions with Dasharatha, Kaikeyi and Lakshmana reveal the human side of the character, while the action sequences establish his capabilities as a warrior.

However, this is one debate where the internet has not entirely changed its mind. Some viewers find his restraint convincing, while others consider it emotionally distant. Yash's Ravana has also emerged as the more immediately celebrated performance. Ranbir's casting scepticism has been challenged, but declaring a unanimous victory would be premature.
The one note that doesn't quite land

For all the surprises, one criticism remains difficult to dismiss: the music. The collaboration between AR Rahman and Hans Zimmer raised expectations considerably. Yet the soundtrack has not generated the same excitement as the film's visuals. Mangal Rang divided listeners over its musical treatment, while Ravana Tandav attracted criticism from those expecting a more powerful and traditional sound.

The background score also struggles to consistently match the emotional and visual scale of the film. There are stretches where the music does not elevate the scene as much as it should. For an epic whose emotional language is so deeply connected to music, this is a significant shortcoming.

Ultimately, Ramayana has not proved that the internet was wrong about everything. It has, however, demonstrated that promotional footage is not a substitute for the finished film. Its VFX has exceeded expectations, its performances have found appreciation, and its quieter moments have given the spectacle an emotional foundation.

The film still has room to improve, particularly in its music, pacing and character development. But perhaps the most interesting takeaway is this: the internet spent months debating whether Ramayana could look like an epic. The theatrical release has shown that, at least visually, it can. Now comes the harder task of making audiences feel the epic as deeply as they see it.
